title: Why Use the Catechisms of the Church?
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This lesson explores the biblical and theological foundations for using catechisms as tools for Christian growth and doctrinal stability. Pastor Lyro defends catechism practice against common objections, demonstrates their historical use in the church, and explains how catechisms serve families and congregations in grounding believers in systematic theology.

outline.title: The Need for Doctrinal Grounding
subpoints: Paul's instruction to Timothy emphasizes passing down faithful teaching to future generations
Believers must be grounded in the gospel to remain unmoved by false doctrine
The church provides teachers to equip Christians and prevent doctrinal drift

outline.title: The Beauty and History of Reformed Catechisms
subpoints: The Heidelberg Catechism presents the comfort of knowing Christ in life and death
Catechisms were structured using the Apostles' Creed, Ten Commandments, and Lord's Prayer
Historical figures like Thomas Watson used catechisms to ground believers in doctrine

outline.title: Addressing Faulty Assumptions About Catechisms
subpoints: Catechism study should complement, not replace, Bible reading
Sola scriptura does not mean rejecting the wisdom of 2,000 years of church teaching
Learning and devotion are not antagonistic; both strengthen faith

outline.title: The Benefits and Safeguards of Catechisms
subpoints: Catechisms provide systematic summaries of biblical teaching on specific topics
They serve as anchors preventing doctrinal drift and heretical interpretation
Catechisms protect against cultic movements that claim novel interpretations
Well-formulated truths help resist falsehoods in an age of confusion

outline.title: The Role of Catechizing in the Home
subpoints: Fathers are called to be priests, prophets, and kings through catechetical instruction
Parents must teach children the mighty acts of God and His faithfulness
Teaching the catechism to children strengthens parents' own faith
Young Timothy learned catechism from his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois

outline.title: The Role of Catechizing in the Church
subpoints: Pastors and elders should support and extend catechetical instruction begun at home
The Sunday School program serves to further catechetical efforts
Systematic theological grounding prevents biblical illiteracy
Catechism practice correlates with biblical literacy in the church

outline.title: Catechisms as a Safeguard Against Error
subpoints: Catechisms provide theological categories for organizing biblical teaching
They give clarity about doctrine and help elders hold teachers accountable
Vague theology allows false teachers to manipulate congregations
Clear doctrinal statements protect congregations from heresy

transcript:
## Why Use Catechisms?

We finished two weeks ago our series on creation, starting with chapter four of our confession. Last week, Craig had an excellent lesson on Romans 5 and the chain of salvation, the chain of justification and sanctification, and how that affects our lives. In two weeks from today, we're going to start a new series—a nine-part series on how the attributes of God, who God is, help us as we deal with anxiety. Anxiety is something that we are all very familiar with. It is one of the top prescribed medications in the United States, though medication cannot truly treat anxiety since it is an issue of the heart.

Today we have a standalone lesson. I love for you to grab your Bible and turn to 2 Timothy chapter 2, verses 1 and 2. The apostle Paul is giving some instruction to Timothy and he says:

> "You therefore my son be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus and the things that you have heard from me among many witnesses commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also."

One of the goals that Paul had in teaching Timothy is that Timothy can teach other people and can catechize other men. Then turn to Colossians chapter 1, verses 21 through 23. Paul says:

> "And you who once were alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death to present you holy and blameless and above reproach in his sight. If indeed you continue in the faith grounded and steadfast and are not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which you heard, which was preached to every creature under heaven of which I, Paul became a minister."

What we see here is this necessity to be grounded in the gospel, to be grounded in theology to be unmovable. In Ephesians 4, the apostle says that one of the reasons why we're part of a church is so that we're not moved by every wind of doctrine.

### The Imagery of Being Grounded

Our neighbor has a huge blue spruce tree that is right on the edge of the property in the front yard. When there's a big storm, that tree sways back and forth, and we hope it doesn't fall our way. It's a different prayer than we pray for the tree here concerning our building. We don't want that tree to fall in our house. If this tree fell on the church, that's not a big deal—we can get a new building out of that with insurance money. But you can see this idea of being moved, right? And that eventually you're going to fall. Or you can have the imagery of being on a boat and going up and down the waves and eventually just getting very sick, which is not conducive for growth, for goodness, for good life and so on. That's the picture that Paul paints for the Christian—that we are supposed to be grounded. We are not supposed to be thrown about by every wind of doctrine.

In Ephesians 4, the context of that passage is that God gave teachers to the church so that that doesn't happen, that you're equipped to do the work of the ministry and help each other grow into the fullness of Christ. And that is what leads to the subject that I wanted to talk about in our Sunday school today. I want to answer the question: Why use catechisms?

## The Beauty of the Heidelberg Catechism

I wanted to start by looking at the beautiful words, perhaps the most beautiful catechism answer in the history of the Reformed church. That's found in the Heidelberg Catechism, Lord's Day 1, which is made of two questions. The Heidelberg Catechism is divided into 52 Lord's Days. The goal of that is that in the afternoon or evening service—because every Dutch church had two services a day—they would teach the doctrine that was in the catechism. It didn't mean that they would read the catechism as their biblical text. They would preach that doctrine from the biblical text.

This is question number 1:

> "What is your only comfort in life and death? That I am not my own, but belong body and soul in life and in death to my faithful savior, Jesus Christ. He has fully paid for all my sins with his precious blood and has set me free from the tyranny of the devil. He also watches over me in such a way that not a hair can fall from my head without the will of my Father in heaven. In fact, all things must work together for my salvation because I belong to him. Christ, by his Holy Spirit, assures me of eternal life and makes me wholeheartedly willing and ready from now on to live for him."

These words are beautiful. These are great words to have committed to memory, to have hanging in your living room, to have with you where you go.

### History of the Heidelberg Catechism

This is the first question of the Heidelberg Catechism, the most revered reformed catechism, written all the way back in 1562 by Zacharias Usinus and Casper Olivianus. Do you want to guess where it was written? In Heidelberg, Germany—yes, that's the name. But with all group projects, you know how what happens with group projects—one person does all the work. Scholars think that actually Usinus is the one that did all the work and Olivianus contributed maybe a couple of periods and commas here and there. The Heidelberg Catechism is a wonderful document of great theological and devotional value. I encourage you to take a look at it and to read from it. Chad Van Dixler edited a volume where he included all the reformation catechisms that have been adopted by denominations with a little introduction and a handsome looking setting of the different catechisms. So I encourage you to get to know the Heidelberg Catechism. It's good for us. Good catechisms are great tools for growth in Christ.

### Thomas Watson and the Shorter Catechism

Thomas Watson was a Presbyterian minister in London right during the time when the Church of England kicked out all the Puritans. In 1662, King Charles II signed the Edict of Conformity, and every pastor in the Church of England would have to use the Book of Common Prayer. Puritans always refused to do that, and one day over 2,000 pastors were kicked out and lost their churches, lost their income, lost their pensions. Thomas Watson was one of them.

One of the things that Thomas Watson would do is that in the afternoon service he would preach through the teachings of the Shorter Catechism, the one that is part of our confession. As a result of that we have three wonderful volumes of his sermons that are based on the Shorter Catechism. The first volume is called the Body of Divinity. The second volume is called the Ten Commandments. The third volume is called the Lord's Prayer, because that's the structure of the catechism.

Do you know why every reformed catechism is structured that way? The outline of every reformed catechism is exactly the same. Do you know why? Because there's this scholastic medieval tendency to structure things in terms of the Apostle's Creed, the Ten Commandments and the Lord's Prayer, and that's how the catechisms are all structured.

In that work Watson says: "Catechizing is the best expedient for the grounding and settling of people. I fear one reason why there has been no more good done by preaching has been because the chief heads and articles in religion have not been explained in the catechetical way. Catechizing is laying the foundation to preach and not catechize is to build without foundation. This way of catechizing is not novel; it is apostolic. The primitive church had their forms of catechism, as those phrases imply a form of some words in 2 Timothy 1:13 and the first principles of the Oracles of God in Hebrews 5:12."

To that we could add at least the five faithful sayings. If you read 1 Timothy and Titus, you are going to find five expressions that are introduced by the phrase "this is a faithful saying." Those were Paul quoting memory work, a summary of doctrines that were circulating the church—catechism for young children that they would memorize so that they would know what is a faithful saying and they would spit out those five things.

## Why Use a Catechism Instead of Just Reading the Bible?

That is the question, right? That's the question I get all the time, and I get that from you, our own people. And I think that's a question that should be asked.

The first thing to say in answering this question is that studying and memorizing a catechism should never replace studying and memorizing the scriptures. So it's not one or the other. We're encouraging everyone to do both. A reformed catechism is an excellent companion to faithful Bible reading.

Now this question seems to be based on two faulty assumptions. The first one is that we have to choose between the two—Bible or catechism. And that's absolutely not the case. We can do both if we desire to do so.

### The Problem of Time

And when I say that, what is the immediate response from people? "Don't have time, right?" If we grabbed your phone and went to the screen that shows where you spent your time on your phone, it wouldn't be on social media or video games or browsing the news. Did you have time to work out this week? Did you have time to watch anything? No matter what it was. So time is not really an issue. Let's just put that away. Time and effort are not usually issues when we want to do something.

### The Second Faulty Assumption: Sola Scriptura Misunderstood

The second faulty assumption is that the doctrine of sola scriptura—the Bible alone, scriptures alone—teaches that we can only know moral and spiritual truth if we read verses from the Bible. We cannot learn anything true from God concerning God unless we are reading from the Bible. This is an understanding of the doctrine of sola scriptura which leads to a "me, Jesus, and the Bible" approach to Bible study, which is not a good approach. It sounds pious, but it's not.

It's me, Jesus, the Bible, and 2,000 years of faithful men and women in the church, helping me to understand this book better. The "me, Jesus, and the Bible" attitude is a very prideful one. The attitude that nobody else who has gone before me matters, that I'm the one that's going to figure everything out, that I don't need anybody else. That's what you're saying when you say the "me, Jesus, and the Bible only" sort of approach. This is not the doctrine of sola scriptura. It's the doctrine of "nuda scriptura"—the scripture is naked without anything.

Our confession recognizes that the scriptures are supreme, but also says that we benefit from the writings of others. In our confession, chapter 1, paragraph 6, it says:

> "The whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life is either expressly set down in scripture or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from scripture."

Then in paragraph 10:

> "The supreme judge by which all controversies of religion are to be determined and all decrees of council, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of man and private spirits are to be examined and in whose sentence we are to rest can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in scripture."

The scriptures are the supreme judge, the ultimate judge, the ultimate authority. But there are other authorities that we follow. The scriptures are the ultimate authority, but there are other authorities that we follow when it comes to faith. For example, the Bible teaches that you are committed to obey your elders. That's an authority, and if you don't obey them, you are sinning because it is authority—not the supreme authority, because the scriptures are the supreme authority.

In God's good providence, he has gifted the church over the centuries with men and women who have been able to search the scriptures and hand down amazing truths to us in distilled form for our benefit. And that's really what the catechism is—things distilled to us in a succinct way for our benefit.

So it is important that we use catechism, and there are benefits from it. Can I say that you're sinning if you don't use the catechism? No, that's not what I'm saying. But I think that it would be foolish not to benefit from the catechisms that the church has produced.

## The Benefits of Reformed Catechisms

### Systematic Summaries of Doctrine

A good reformed catechism provides a truthful and systematic summary of the Bible's teaching on a specific topic. Again, Watson says: "Knowledge of principles is to the soul as an anchor is to the ship—it holds it steady in the midst of the rolling waves of error or violent winds of persecutions." Catechisms are supposed to be anchors; memorizing them, knowing them, helps us to be anchored there.

A good reformed catechism provides a bite-sized answer to important topics. Unless you're memorizing the Larger Catechism—then it's not quite a bite-size, more like a plate-size. For example, instead of memorizing every verse in the Bible about sin in order to say something about sin, you can use a summary that the catechism gives you. Shorter Catechism, Question 14 asks:

> "What is sin?"

And the answer is:

> "Sin is any want of conformity unto or transgression of the law of God."

So sin is any lack of conformity—not doing what the Bible says we're supposed to do—or transgression, doing the things the Bible tells us not to do—of the law of God. So instead of memorizing every verse, we can have this summary there.

Brothers and sisters, we all do that. If I ask you what sin is and you give an answer that is holistic and that includes the teaching of the Bible, guess what you just did? You created a summary of what that doctrine is. It's so helpful to have these well-formulated truths when we are being bombarded with falsehoods.

A good reformed catechism also has been widely adopted and tested by time and use. I'm not for new catechisms because those haven't been tested yet. Tim Keller put out the New City Catechism a few years ago and a lot of churches adopted it as being the best thing ever. Let's wait 100 years and make sure that it's still around and that the church has really approved it before we do anything with that.

### Theological Categories and Organization

Theological categories given to us through catechism help us make sense of the myriad details in the scriptures. The Bible is a big book. It's difficult to keep everything in order, organized in our heads, and the catechisms help us keep those things organized.

### Protection Against Heresy

The practice of catechism also serves as an important safeguard against heresy and helps to mitigate some of the problems associated with the private interpretation of scripture.

Do you know how every Christian cult starts? See it? A guy with a Bible saying we don't need anything else. I know what's best. I have new ideas that come from the Bible. It's interesting that new revelation is not the first claim. It's new interpretation that's the first claim. "We don't need anything else, and you don't listen to anybody else. If somebody says something different than what I'm saying, don't listen to them. Only my interpretation."

That's really how every cult in America began—with an open Bible and a charismatic leader who ensures his or her followers that they alone had discovered what everyone else, especially the creeds, confessions and catechisms, had missed. And when we mention that, we see greater value in our catechisms. These guides protect us from these errors and protect us also from these self-deluded teachers.

### Clarity and Accountability

And you know what I think it does? It gives clarity. I can go to Darren and to Scott and to Nick and say, when they say something, we can go to them or we can go to each other and say, "You swore, you took a vow saying that you believe in the system of doctrine presented in the Shorter Catechism. The Shorter Catechism says this, but you are teaching this. You are breaking your vows. How do you explain that?"

So clarity is in place. A lot of times that's why people don't like catechism because it brings clarity. And they want to live in a place of muddled belief where they can control people.

### The Connection Between Catechism and Biblical Literacy

As American evangelicalism has moved away from the practice of catechism for subjective and experiential modes of meaning, it is no accident that biblical literacy has gone down. Do you get that? The more people use the catechism, the more they know the Bible. The less they use the catechism, the less they know the Bible. That's the historical trend that we see there.

## Catechizing in the Home

The practice of catechizing is ideally a two-fold emphasis: family and church.

### The Role of Fathers

The first of these emphases centers around the home. If Christian men wonder about their primary role as fathers in terms of their obligation to be priests, prophets, and kings in the home, I suggest that the practice of catechizing plays a major role in your duties.

The scriptures make it very clear that parents, especially fathers, are assigned the role of recounting to their children the mighty acts of God in redeeming His people. In Exodus 12-13, we have Passover instituted in chapter 12. Chapter 13 comes later on when we get the Promised Land—things are settled. There's a long distance between what's happening here and there, and your child comes and asks you, "Why are we doing this?" Be ready to answer that question. That's teaching in question-and-answer format done by the Father. That predates Aristotle.

God commands us to teach his commands to your children and your grandchildren. We see that practiced in Deuteronomy 4, in Psalm 78, in Joshua 8. I want to call attention to Joshua 8. Here we have Joshua reading the whole book of Deuteronomy to everybody together, and they're being instructed systematically. And I want you to notice at the end there, which says:

> "Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel... a word of all that Moses had commanded, which Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, women, the little ones, the strangers who were living among them."

Notice how the Holy Spirit details who the audience of the teaching was—women, the little ones, the strangers who were living among them. So the teaching of the word is happening everywhere, including to the little ones.

The prophet Isaiah tells us that parents are to tell their children about God's faithfulness. Isaiah 38 says:

> "The living man, he shall praise you as I do this day, the Father shall make known your truth to the children."

In the New Testament we discover that the young pastor Timothy had learned these things from whom? Remember? Lois and Eunice. Who were they? His mother and grandmother, right? Being catechized at home. And Paul tells the parents that they are to bring the children up in the church and in the admonition of the Lord, specifically the fathers, to do that. Our children come to Christ often directly through instruction in the home. That's why catechizing is so important.

### The Benefit to Parents

Parents, there might be a benefit to you. There is a great benefit to you in doing that. What happens when you are teaching your children the catechism? What's the best way to learn something? To teach it, right? So as you're working on catechizing your children, you are catechized yourself as well, and there's a great benefit in doing that.

## Catechizing in the Church

The second emphasis of catechizing centers on the role of the church. The role of the pastor and elders as well as the goal of the Sunday School program should be to further and support those efforts at catechizing that have ideally begun in the home. But parents should not assume that the church's role is to supply all the catechical instruction. Parents are to work with the children at home.

The best way for Christians to be settled in their faith is to be well-grounded in that faith's theology. Again, Watson says: "We can never worship God acceptably unless we worship Him regularly. And how can we do that if we are ignorant of the rules and elements of religion?"

This systematic grounding that catechizing brings is the best way to be settled in our religion. Religion is not a bad word, by the way. It's a good word.

So if we want our children to grow up to be men and women of God, one of the best possible ways for this to happen is to recover the practice of catechism. And we too, if we want to be better, greater men and women of God, we must avail ourselves of those wonderful resources that God in His providence has given to us.

### A Powerful Example

We have a nephew who struggles with enslavement to drugs. And so he's often not of a sound mind. But in moments of lucidity, moments where his mind is there, the things he remembers the most is his mom, when he was a little kid, five, six, maybe even younger, teaching him the catechism. In all the turmoil that drugs and whatever other things have brought to his mind, what sometimes grounds him was the catechetical effort of his mother. And that shows the power of the systematic learning of the scriptures there.
